title: Crushing chest pain
stem: 58-year-old man, smoker with high blood pressure. 40 minutes of crushing central chest pain spreading to his left arm and jaw, sweating, nauseous. BP 152/94 in both arms, HR 104.
expert: Acute coronary syndrome (heart attack)
Classic pressure-type pain radiating to arm and jaw, sweating, nausea, plus risk factors (smoking, hypertension, male, 58). Most likely AND most dangerous. ECG within 10 minutes and troponin.
Aortic dissection
Can't-miss. Usually tearing pain to the back with a big blood pressure difference between arms. Equal BPs make it less likely, but it still has to be thought about before giving blood thinners.
Pulmonary embolism
Chest pain + fast heart rate. Less likely without breathlessness, low oxygen or clot risk factors, but deadly if missed.
Pericarditis
Sharp pain, better sitting forward, often after a virus. Crushing pain with arm radiation doesn't fit well.
GERD (acid reflux)
Burning pain after meals. Common, but you only settle on it after ruling out the heart.
others: Pain you can reproduce by pressing on the chest wall; no sweating or arm spread.
A diagnosis of exclusion; never assume it in a 58-year-old smoker with crushing pain.
Sudden sharp one-sided pain with breathlessness, often tall thin young people.

title: Worst headache of my life
stem: 42-year-old woman. Sudden headache that hit maximum in seconds while lifting a box, "the worst of my life". Vomited twice, neck feels stiff. No fever.
expert: Subarachnoid hemorrhage

Thunderclap onset (peak within a minute), worst ever, vomiting, neck stiffness from blood irritating the meninges. Usually a burst berry aneurysm. CT head first; if CT is normal, lumbar puncture for xanthochromia.
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome
Repeated thunderclap headaches from arteries going into spasm, often triggered by exertion. Diagnosed with vessel imaging.
Cervical artery dissection
A tear in a neck artery can cause sudden head/neck pain and later a stroke. Look for neck pain and Horner syndrome.
Bacterial meningitis
Neck stiffness and headache, but usually builds over hours with fever. No fever here, so lower.
Migraine
Common, but migraines build over minutes to hours. Thunderclap onset is NOT a migraine until proven otherwise.
others: Band-like, mild to moderate, no vomiting, never thunderclap.
Facial pressure and congestion, gradual onset.
Stabbing pain around one eye with a watery eye, in men more often, attacks 15–180 min.

title: Belly pain moving to the right
stem: 16-year-old boy. Pain started around his belly button yesterday, now sharp in the lower right. Lost his appetite, vomited once, temp 38.2 °C. Pain when he coughs.
expert: Appendicitis
Textbook migration from around the belly button to the right lower quadrant (McBurney's point), anorexia, low fever, pain with coughing (peritoneal irritation). Ultrasound or CT, then appendectomy.
Mesenteric adenitis
Swollen lymph nodes in the gut lining after a virus, can mimic appendicitis in kids and teens. Usually there's a recent sore throat or cold.
Gastroenteritis
Vomiting and pain, but diarrhea is usually prominent and pain is spread out, not focused.
Crohn's disease (terminal ileum)
Right lower pain, but usually weeks of diarrhea, weight loss and tiredness.
Kidney stone (right ureter)
Colicky flank-to-groin pain, can't sit still, blood in urine. Not the migrating pattern.
others: Can refer pain to the belly in kids, but expect cough and fast breathing.
Pain with movement, no fever or vomiting.

title: Breathless after a flight
stem: 31-year-old woman, flew 13 hours yesterday. Sudden sharp right chest pain worse when breathing in, short of breath. HR 112, oxygen 91%. Right calf is swollen.
expert: Pulmonary embolism
Long flight (immobility), swollen calf (DVT), sudden pleuritic pain, fast heart rate, low oxygen. CT pulmonary angiogram; treated with anticoagulants.
Pneumothorax
Sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness; check for absent breath sounds on one side. Chest X-ray.
Pneumonia
Pleuritic pain and low oxygen, but usually fever and productive cough over days.
Acute coronary syndrome
Less likely at 31 with pleuritic pain, but an ECG and troponin are cheap and fast.
Pericarditis
Sharp pain but better leaning forward; ECG shows widespread ST elevation.
others: Wheeze and tight chest; doesn't explain the swollen calf.
Never the first answer with low oxygen and a swollen leg.

title: Fever, stiff neck, confused
stem: 19-year-old college student in a dorm. 12 hours of fever, severe headache, stiff neck, light hurts his eyes, now confused. A purple rash that doesn't fade when pressed.
expert: Bacterial meningitis (meningococcal)

Fever + stiff neck + confusion is meningitis until proven otherwise, and a non-blanching purple rash in a dorm student screams Neisseria meningitidis. Give IV antibiotics immediately (don't wait for the scan or LP).
Meningococcal sepsis
The same bacteria in the blood; the rash is bleeding into the skin. Can kill within hours.
Viral meningitis
Similar symptoms but usually milder, no confusion, no purple rash.
HSV encephalitis
Fever + confusion + behaviour change or seizures; affects the temporal lobes. Treated with acyclovir.
Subarachnoid hemorrhage
Stiff neck and headache, but sudden onset without fever.
others: No fever, no rash, no confusion.
Fever and headache but no neck stiffness or rash.
Builds over days to weeks, focal signs.

title: Arm weak, can't talk
stem: 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation. Woke normal; at 9:10 AM his right arm and face suddenly went weak and he can't get words out. Glucose 112.
expert: Ischemic stroke (left MCA)
Sudden right face + arm weakness with aphasia = left middle cerebral artery territory. Atrial fibrillation throws clots. Time is brain: CT to exclude bleeding, then clot-busting drug or thrombectomy.
Intracerebral hemorrhage
Looks identical at the bedside; only the CT tells them apart. That's why the scan comes BEFORE clot-busters.
Todd's paralysis after a seizure
Weakness after an unwitnessed seizure can mimic a stroke; usually resolves within 48 h.
Hypoglycemia
The classic stroke mimic, which is why glucose is checked first. Normal here, so ruled down.
Migraine with aura
Can cause temporary weakness or speech trouble, usually spreading slowly with a headache, in younger people.
others: Symptoms build over weeks, not seconds.
Face only (including the forehead), no arm weakness or aphasia.

title: Legs getting weaker
stem: 26-year-old man. Food poisoning with diarrhea 2 weeks ago. Now 4 days of tingling feet and weakness climbing from his legs to his hips. Knee and ankle reflexes are gone.
expert: Guillain-Barré syndrome

Ascending weakness + lost reflexes after an infection (Campylobacter diarrhea is classic). Antibodies attack peripheral nerve myelin. LP shows high protein with normal cells. Treated with IVIG or plasma exchange; watch breathing.
Spinal cord compression
Leg weakness can come from the cord, but expect a sensory level, back pain and bladder trouble, with brisk reflexes later.
Transverse myelitis
Inflamed spinal cord: weakness, a sensory level and bladder problems.
Myasthenia gravis
Weakness that gets worse with use, eyes and face first; reflexes are normal.
Hypokalemia
Low potassium causes weakness after diarrhea; check a BMP. Doesn't usually cause tingling that climbs.
others: DEScending weakness starting with eyes and swallowing.
One side of the body, sudden.
Episodes with upper motor neuron signs (brisk reflexes).

title: Thirsty, losing weight
stem: 12-year-old girl. 3 weeks of drinking lots, peeing a lot (wetting the bed again), weight loss. Today vomiting with belly pain, breath smells fruity, breathing deep.
expert: Diabetic ketoacidosis (new type 1 diabetes)

Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss = high blood sugar; fruity breath (acetone), deep Kussmaul breathing and vomiting = ketoacidosis. Check glucose, ketones and a blood gas. Treat with fluids, insulin, potassium.
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
Very high sugar without much ketosis; much more typical in older adults with type 2.
Gastroenteritis
Vomiting and belly pain, but doesn't explain 3 weeks of thirst and weight loss.
Diabetes insipidus
Peeing and thirst, but blood sugar is normal and there's no fruity breath.
Appendicitis
DKA belly pain can mimic it. Fix the DKA and re-examine.
others: Can cause bedwetting, but not weight loss and ketone breath.
Weight loss and fast heart rate, but not ketoacidosis.

title: Barking cough at night
stem: 2-year-old with a runny nose for 2 days; tonight a cough that sounds like a seal barking, a harsh noise when breathing in. Low fever, still drinking.
expert: Croup (viral laryngotracheobronchitis)

Barking cough + inspiratory stridor + cold symptoms in a toddler = croup, usually parainfluenza virus. Swelling below the vocal cords. Treated with a steroid; nebulized epinephrine (adrenaline) if severe.
Inhaled foreign body
Toddlers put things in their mouths. Sudden choking episode then cough or stridor. Can't-miss.
Epiglottitis
Can't-miss: high fever, drooling, sitting forward, toxic, no barky cough. Rare since the Hib vaccine.
Bacterial tracheitis
Looks like croup but the child is very sick with a high fever and doesn't improve with treatment.
Anaphylaxis
Stridor from throat swelling, but with hives, sudden onset after a trigger.
others: Wheeze when breathing OUT, not stridor breathing in.
Coughing fits with a "whoop", lasting weeks.

title: Grandpa getting confused
stem: 79-year-old man on a blood thinner for atrial fibrillation. Fell and hit his head 3 weeks ago. Over the past week: headaches, sleepier, confused, left leg dragging.
expert: Chronic subdural hematoma

Elderly (brain shrinks, stretching bridging veins) + blood thinner + fall weeks ago + slowly worsening confusion and one-sided weakness. CT shows a crescent of dark/grey blood. Often drained through burr holes.
Ischemic stroke
One-sided weakness in an AF patient, but stroke is sudden, not over a week.
Delirium from infection
UTI or pneumonia can cause confusion in elderly people, but not a dragging leg.
Brain tumor
Slowly worsening deficits; the fall and blood thinner make bleeding more likely.
Hyponatremia
Low sodium can cause confusion; check a BMP.
others: Develops over months to years, not a week.
Slow tremor and stiffness over years.

title: Cough and fever
stem: 67-year-old man. 3 days of fever, shaking chills, cough with yellow-green sputum, sharp pain when breathing on the right. Crackles at the right base. Oxygen 92%.
expert: Community-acquired pneumonia
Fever + productive cough + pleuritic pain + focal crackles + low oxygen. Chest X-ray shows consolidation. Most common bug: Streptococcus pneumoniae. Antibiotics.
Acute bronchitis
Cough with sputum but no focal crackles, normal oxygen, usually viral.
Pulmonary embolism
Pleuritic pain and low oxygen; less likely with fever and productive cough.
Heart failure
Crackles and breathlessness, but on both sides, with leg swelling, no fever.
Lung cancer with infection
A tumor can block an airway and cause pneumonia behind it; consider in smokers if it doesn't clear.
others: Weeks of cough, night sweats, weight loss.
Can cause cough but not fever and crackles.

title: Droopy eyelids by evening
stem: 35-year-old woman. For 2 months her eyelids droop and she sees double, worse in the evening and after reading, better after resting. Sometimes tired chewing.
expert: Myasthenia gravis

Fatigable weakness (worse with use, better with rest) of eyes then bulbar muscles. Antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Test: acetylcholine receptor antibodies; treated with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine) and immunotherapy. Check for a thymoma.
Lambert-Eaton syndrome
Neuromuscular junction too, but weakness IMPROVES with use, legs first, and often linked to lung cancer.
Thyroid eye disease
Double vision and eye changes, but eyes bulge and it doesn't fluctuate through the day.
Third nerve palsy (aneurysm)
Can't-miss: droopy lid + double vision + a blown pupil. Not fatigable.
Multiple sclerosis
Can cause double vision, but in episodes with other neuro signs, not daily fatigue.
others: Small droopy lid with a small pupil, no double vision.
Rapid descending paralysis with dilated pupils.
Can't close the eye; lid doesn't droop.
